item.title: SMB — NTLMv2
item.description:
serve "smb" { addr = "0.0.0.0:445" }

The password never crosses the wire: a client sends a proof computed from it. The share tells a reader they are one — in the access mask, before they try, rather than by failing a write later.

What a directory must hold

NTLMv2 needs the password itself or its MD4 (sambaNTPassword, an nt_hash column). Nothing else will do.

A directory that only checks passwords — an LDAP bind, a bcrypt column —cannot answer SMB, however good the check is, because the server has to compute the same proof the client did. That is a property of the protocol, not a limitation of this program.

check prints a - in the SMB column for such a person, at configuration time, rather than leaving them to discover it at a mount.

Kerberos: a ticket instead of a password 

kerberos {
 realm = "EXAMPLE.ORG"
 keytab = "/etc/fileshare/krb5.keytab" # nfs/fs.example.org and cifs/fs.example.org
}

serve "smb" {
 addr = "0.0.0.0:445"
 ntlm = false # Kerberos only: no password is ever checked
}

The kerberos block that lets NFS tell people apart also lets SMB take a ticket. One keytab holds both services, each protocol answering for its own:SMB reads only the cifs/<host> principals of the block’s realm, so a ticket made for nfs/ is refused here. A keytab with no cifs/ principal leaves SMB as it was, NTLM only, and the server says so at startup.

The principal goes through the same rule as over NFS (another realm’s alice is nobody) and must then be somebody this configuration knows: a ticket proves the KDC knows the person, not that this server does. The share’s allow andwriters lists apply as for a password. A session ends with its ticket, and a Windows client authenticates again by itself.

Since fileshare v0.50.0 the keytab must be a regular file, owned by root or by the account fileshare runs as, and neither readable or writable by others nor writable by its group: root:fileshare 0640 and fileshare:fileshare 0600 are accepted, krb5:fileshare 0640 is refused. This applies to SMB and NFS. The client’s name and realm are taken from the ticket, never from the authenticator the client also sends (jcmturner/gokrb5#577, RFC 4120 section 3.2.3); NFS needs go-authn/krb5 v0.3.4 or later, which v0.50.0 ships.

ntlm = false is refused at load without a kerberos block, and the server refuses to start if the keytab holds no cifs/ key for the realm: a server nobody can log in to is not one. With it, a person whose directory holds no NT hash can still use SMB, and check says so.

A Windows machine that is not in a domain reaches it with a ticket from this realm: ksetup /addkdc and ksetup /addhosttorealmmap once, a ticket-granting ticket in the logon session, and net use \\fs.example.org\photos — by name,since Windows falls back to NTLM for an address. Measured with Windows 11 25H2(not joined): the client offers MS-KRB5, Kerberos, NEGOEX and NTLMSSP, sends a Kerberos AP-REQ, mounts, lists, reads and writes with signing required, and sends no NTLM message at all.

SMB over QUIC 

tls {
 cert_file = "/var/lib/caddy/certificates/acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org-directory/files.example.org/files.example.org.crt"
 key_file = "/var/lib/caddy/certificates/acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org-directory/files.example.org/files.example.org.key"
}

serve "smb" {
 addr = ":443" # UDP: it does not clash with an HTTPS proxy on TCP 443
 transport = "quic"
 tls = true
 # client_cert = "required"
 # client_ca_file = "/etc/fileshare/client-ca.pem"
}

SMB 3.1.1 over QUIC is the same protocol inside TLS 1.3 on UDP 443, with ALPNsmb: net use \\files.example.org\share /TRANSPORT:QUIC on Windows 11, with TCP 445 closed. The certificate is the tls block’s and its files are reloaded when they change, so pointing them at a reverse proxy’s ACME storage follows its renewals. A Windows client checks the server name against the certificate’s DNS names: dial a name, never an address (an address also forces NTLM). A proxy on the same host must not offer HTTP/3 on that UDP port (Caddy: protocols h1 h2).

By default only Kerberos tells people apart, with a cifs/files.example.org principal in the keytab. client_cert = "required" adds a client certificate chaining to client_ca_file, demanded in the TLS handshake before any SMB byte is read: it says which machine may connect, the Kerberos principal is still who the person is. The CA file is read when the server starts. Over QUIC the server grants one credit per request and advertises no large MTU ([MS-SMB2] 3.3.5.4),so a read or write is at most 64 KiB. identity = "system" and isolated children do not serve QUIC yet and the server refuses to start with them. Oneserve "smb" block carries one transport: run a second instance for TCP.

A privileged port without a privileged server

Under --isolate on Unix, the parent binds 445 and passes the listener to the child, so the process actually speaking SMB never needs the privilege. Windows has no ExtraFiles, so there the child binds the address itself; the isolation is the same, the privileged-port half is not.

Verified against a client this project did not write

go-smb2 drives twenty concurrent reads through SMB while twenty run through WebDAV, under -race, in CI. macOS mounts a share over SMB while curl writes to the same image over WebDAV, and reads back what WebDAV wrote.

When the people change

SMB fixes who may connect to a share when the share is added, and checks it once per tree connect. So somebody new whom a directory reload finds is added in place, SMB’s running server included, with no connection touched; but anything taken away — a person, a credential, a share’s expanded lists — is a new generation, and SMB’s open connections are closed, so a revocation reaches the sessions already open. A share whose allow group has emptied is not offered over SMB at all: its empty AllowUsers would read as everyone.

Requests in flight

Since go-filesystems/smb v0.8.1 a connection holds up to 32 requests in flight, and the server up to 128 across all connections. Replies are matched by MessageId. A frame holding one READ of a plain file runs beside others; compound chains (answered whole, in order), asynchronous requests and WRITE run alone. A frame has 30 s to arrive once it has begun. The mechanism is the shared module go-filesystems/inflight, also used by SFTP and NFS.
